approved: Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would turn Australia's commitments under a global ocean biodiversity treaty into domestic law.
It creates a new regulatory system covering marine genetic resources, area-based management tools and environmental impact assessments for waters beyond any country's control.
The compliance framework would adopt standard provisions from the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Act 2014, with minor modifications.
Implements obligations from Parts II, III and IV of the BBNJ Agreement into Australian law.
Establishes a modern compliance and enforcement framework using standard Commonwealth regulatory powers.
Allows information collected under the bill to be shared with state, territory and other Australian Government bodies.
Provides legislative authority for Commonwealth spending to implement the BBNJ Agreement.
Australian government agencies, industries such as tourism, fishing and aquaculture, and individuals operating in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

Moved to introduce the High Seas Biodiversity Bill 2026, giving effect to the United Nations agreement on conserving and sustainably using marine biological diversity beyond national jurisdiction; the question was agreed to and the bill was read a first time.

Supported the High Seas Biodiversity Bill 2026 as a framework for implementing Australia's treaty obligations, protecting ocean biodiversity and regulating Australian activities beyond national jurisdiction. Contributions highlighted bipartisan cooperation, enforcement concerns, marine protected areas, environmental assessments, international cooperation and Australia's planned ratification.

Argued that the High Seas Biodiversity Bill 2026 would ratify the United Nations high seas treaty, establish frameworks for marine protected areas, benefit sharing and environmental impact assessments, and support ocean protection; speakers supported the bill as a step toward protecting marine biodiversity and addressing interconnected local and global ocean pressures.

Argued that the High Seas Biodiversity Bill 2026 would enable Australia to ratify the BBNJ Agreement, strengthen protection of marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, support ocean businesses and research, and reinforce regional cooperation and Australia's role as an ocean leader.

Argued that the High Seas Biodiversity Bill 2026 should protect biodiversity while recognising the fishing industry's sustainability, food-security role and need for genuine consultation, and warned that the treaty must not be used to impose further domestic fishing closures without proper assessment.
